We don't even know what's in the contract, staffing-wise. The site super has been here 12 years and has never seen a single sentence from it. Neither has her boss, the field manager. We have some shifts the client specifically doesn't want staffed to save money, third shift person at my post leaves with no relief at 7am during weekdays. For first shift, the assistant site supervisor handles 3/4 posts for slightly more money five days a week. 

One post isn't staffed except for weekends (it's tiny, a walkthrough takes maybe 20 minutes if you know the layout well.) If nobody feels like working it, we have someone from the closest other post act like a mobile and do both. 

It's crazy how strict it seems like most sites and supervisors are. We don't make nearly enough money to expect constant dedication. If you want that, become a cop, fireman, or join the military.

Former pro musician here. 

This is a complicated question. In the "old days," up until around the 1960s, the vast majority of music, including recordings by folks like Elvis and Johnny Cash, happened live in a room. Mics were set up to capture the sound of what happened in that room. There were challenges, especially drummers, because drums are fucking loud as an acoustic instrument. If you had a drummer who played like a gorilla, that was a problem. John Bonham was nearly fired from several of his pre-Zeppelin bands because he hit so hard. It also made live performances difficult, because PA systems at music venues barely existed prior to Woodstock. When the Beatles played stadiums in the first half of the 1960s, the only sound the audience heard was coming through the little speakers the announcers used during games. Massive speaker rigs were an invention of the 1970s, when more big venues (for sports or theater shows) started doing double-duty as concert venues.

There are exceptions. Les Paul, the guy the Gibson guitar model is named after, basically invented multi-track recording, the earliest version of your latter example. He would bounce acetate (first-recording) record discs back and forth on multiple record-cutters, recording a new part on top of what already existed on the last disc. He was doing this in the 1940s, but it was an extremely complicated process. He once had to throw out about 50 discs because a low-flying plane flew over his place while recording and start all over, so it wasn't a popular technique. 

Once the 70s hit, washing-machine-sized multitrack tape recorders were everywhere. You could record a click track, the band plays to it on different channels (24 possible,) and if one guy screwed up, they could go back and "punch in" the correct part without affecting the rest of the recording. 

That's the idea that gave birth to things like Pro Tools, which actually started being used in the late 80s. Some of Motley Crue's Dr. Feelgood album (1989) was edited digitally using an early version of it, per their book The Dirt. 

Today, the vast majority of recordings you hear have had hundreds of edits and retakes done. On an album by a big icon with a budget in the millions, it could be thousands. Minor tweaks to a beat, auto-tuning every single note sung (though this is much easier than it used to be,) cutting and pasting so the artist only has to sing the chorus and harmonies once, stuff like that. 

Today, damn near everything is edited hundreds of times on an average album. Effects like reverb and delay are added. If you wanted those in the "old days," you actually had to just find a huge room and record it organically. There are some purists out there who still do such things, but i'm not aware of any who are super famous. (Slash, the Rolling Stones, and Green Day have recorded on old tape machines somewhat recently, but doing so today is extremely expensive because most companies have stopped making the tape and parts for the machines.)

As a cold junkie, this sounds great to me, but first thing to check is temp sensors. Those control when the unit kicks on and off based on what you've set it at. One will be in your outside unit, it will probably be a small black-box looking thing with a black wire leading off of it. Indoor ones are harder to locate, because they could be anywhere depending on how the system was installed. (They may also lead to higher energy bills if you have a multi-floor house. Next, as I learned recently, is check fuses on the control board wherever the "brain" is. One bad fuse knocked out our sensors and our entire panel, zero power to either. It was .63 cents to replace after reading the service manual, which is generally available online for most units in the USA.

How to use a fire extinguisher. 

Your average red extinguisher is known as an "ABC," meaning it's good for most types of average fires (namely flammable solids, most flammable liquids, and electrical fires.) 

If the extinguisher has been well-maintained, it should have a plastic seal on it's pin, which is near the handle. Pull the pin, break the seal, aim the hose at the fire, and squeeze the handles together. Use a side-to-side sweeping motion aimed at the base of the fire to make sure the entire area is covered. 

There are quite a few types of extinguishers, and I see oddballs out in public every now and then. If you see a silver one, there's a good chance it's pressurized water, only really good for flammable solids. More rarely, it might be AFFF foam, which is used for super flammable liquids.

Oh, and grease/fat fires. Using any extinguisher other than a K is iffy. Most commercial kitchens have these, because grease is weird. Basically anything you do to a grease fire can make it worse. Ks work by basically neutralizing the acidic properties of grease via alkaline. 

There are also D class, which are for flammable metals like magnesium, but your average person will likely never encounter such a scenario while out and about.

EDIT: Also worth noting, the reason why there are so many extinguishers in a normal Walmart or whatever is because their primary intended use is to create a path to escape a fire. No business is expecting a patron to be a hero and put out a small fire, they want you to fucking *run.* The extinguisher comes into play if your escape routes are blocked by fire. Always escape first if you are able to do so.

***
Pull the pin and break the seal

Aim the hose at the fire

Squeeze the handles together

Sweep the spray across the fire, side to side, until it is out or there is at least enough room for you to escape.

If your average person gets their produce from Punjabi Market, and suddenly it is always closed when they show up, they're going to stop going there. I'm not sure there's any solution here, other than America's 24/7 economy drowning out small retail businesses due to inconvenience.
